canonical_statement: The 2024 guideline is a focused update of the lupus nephritis chapter of the KDIGO 2021 Glomerular Diseases guideline, intended to assist clinicians caring for people with lupus nephritis and focused mainly on treatment evidence published since the prior update.
KDIGO used a Work Group with nephrology and methods expertise and a Brown University Evidence Review Team to update systematic evidence reviews for lupus nephritis.

Clinical questions were structured in PICOD format. The 2024 treatment update prioritized randomized controlled trials published in peer-reviewed journals, with systematic reviews conducted using Cochrane methods and certainty assessed with GRADE.

For the concurrent lupus nephritis and ANCA update, 1,556 records were screened. Twenty-one new eligible lupus nephritis articles were included, representing 16 new randomized trials in 17 publications plus 4 new analyses of previously included trials; the total lupus nephritis review included 97 randomized trials and 16 observational studies.

Recommendation strength used Level 1, 'we recommend,' or Level 2, 'we suggest,' with evidence certainty graded A through D. Practice Points were ungraded consensus guidance. The final draft underwent external public review and was revised before Work Group approval.

KDIGO provides a surveillance and biopsy pathway for kidney involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus. At SLE presentation and during regular surveillance, test serum creatinine and eGFR, urinalysis with sediment, spot protein-creatinine ratio, anti-dsDNA, and complement. Quantify abnormal proteinuria, repeat abnormal kidney function testing, and consider kidney biopsy when 24-hour proteinuria is at least 500 mg/day or when unexplained kidney dysfunction persists.
KDIGO recommends hydroxychloroquine or an equivalent antimalarial for patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, including lupus nephritis, unless contraindicated. The recommendation is graded 1C.

Adjunctive measures should be considered for all patients with lupus nephritis to reduce cardiovascular, kidney, infection, bone, ultraviolet-light, fertility, pregnancy, and malignancy risks associated with the disease or its treatment.

For Class I or II lupus nephritis with low-level proteinuria, immunosuppression should be guided by extrarenal SLE manifestations. Nephrotic syndrome should prompt evaluation for lupus podocytopathy, treatment as minimal change disease when appropriate, and consideration of low-dose glucocorticoid plus another immunosuppressive agent for maintenance.

KDIGO recommends initial glucocorticoids plus one of four options for active Class III or IV lupus nephritis, with or without a membranous component: a mycophenolic acid analog, low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide, belimumab plus a mycophenolic acid analog or low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide, or a mycophenolic acid analog plus a calcineurin inhibitor when kidney function is not severely impaired. Each option is graded 1B. The printed recommendation defines the kidney-function parenthetical as eGFR less than or equal to 45 mL/min/1.73 m2, while Figure 5 uses eGFR greater than 45 mL/min/1.73 m2 for voclosporin; this internal inconsistency is preserved and flagged.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: A reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen after a short course of methylprednisolone pulses may be considered during initial treatment of active lupus nephritis when kidney and extrarenal disease manifestations improve satisfactorily.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: Intravenous cyclophosphamide can be used as initial therapy for active Class III or IV lupus nephritis when adherence to an oral regimen may be difficult.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: A mycophenolic acid analog based regimen is preferred as initial therapy for proliferative lupus nephritis in patients at high risk of infertility, including those with moderate-to-high prior cyclophosphamide exposure.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: A calcineurin inhibitor containing initial regimen may be preferred in patients with relatively preserved kidney function and nephrotic-range proteinuria likely related to extensive podocyte injury, and in patients who cannot tolerate standard-dose mycophenolic acid analog therapy or will not use cyclophosphamide.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: Belimumab with glucocorticoids plus either a mycophenolic acid analog or reduced-dose cyclophosphamide may be preferred in patients with repeated kidney flares or high risk of progression to kidney failure because of severe chronic kidney disease.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: Azathioprine or leflunomide with glucocorticoids may be considered when standard initial drugs are not tolerated, available, or affordable, but these alternatives may have inferior efficacy, more flares, or more drug toxicity.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: Rituximab may be considered for persistent disease activity or an inadequate response to initial standard-of-care therapy; additional biologic and non-biologic therapies remain under development.

source_anchor.section: Class III or IV initial therapy

canonical_statement: After completion of initial therapy, KDIGO recommends a mycophenolic acid analog for maintenance therapy. The recommendation is graded 1B.

Azathioprine is an alternative to a mycophenolic acid analog for maintenance after initial therapy when mycophenolic acid analogs are not tolerated or available, or when pregnancy is being considered.

Glucocorticoids should be tapered to the lowest possible maintenance dose unless needed for extrarenal lupus. Discontinuation can be considered after a complete clinical renal response has been maintained for at least 12 months.
Early maintenance dosing is approximately mycophenolate mofetil 750 to 1000 mg twice daily or mycophenolic acid 540 to 720 mg twice daily.
The combined duration of initial immunosuppression and maintenance combination immunosuppression for proliferative lupus nephritis should be at least 36 months.
Patients treated with triple immunosuppressive regimens that include belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor may continue a triple regimen during maintenance.
If mycophenolic acid analogs and azathioprine cannot be used for maintenance, a calcineurin inhibitor, mizoribine, or leflunomide can be considered.

For pure Class V lupus nephritis, low-level proteinuria is managed with monitoring, renin-angiotensin system blockade and blood pressure control, hydroxychloroquine, and immunosuppression guided by extrarenal SLE. Nephrotic-range proteinuria warrants combined immunosuppression with glucocorticoid plus another agent such as a mycophenolic acid analog, cyclophosphamide, or a calcineurin inhibitor, with moderate or reduced glucocorticoid dosing preferred.

KDIGO points to trial response definitions: complete response requires protein-creatinine ratio below 0.5 g/g with stable or improved kidney function, usually within 6 to 12 months; primary efficacy renal response uses protein-creatinine ratio at or below 0.7 g/g with preserved eGFR and no rescue therapy; partial response requires at least a 50% proteinuria reduction to below 3 g/g with stable or improved kidney function; no kidney response is failure to achieve partial or complete response within 6 to 12 months.

For unsatisfactory response, verify adherence, ensure adequate immunosuppressive dosing and drug exposure when measurable, repeat kidney biopsy if chronicity or another diagnosis is a concern, switch to an alternative recommended regimen for persistent active disease, and consider rituximab or another biologic, an extended intravenous cyclophosphamide course, or clinical-trial enrollment for refractory disease.
After complete or partial remission, a lupus nephritis relapse should be treated with the same initial therapy that achieved the original response or with another recommended therapy.

Lupus nephritis with thrombotic microangiopathy should be managed according to the TMA cause. The algorithm uses ADAMTS13 testing and antiphospholipid antibodies to distinguish thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, antiphospholipid syndrome nephropathy, complement-mediated TMA, and other causes, with cause-specific plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, rituximab, caplacizumab, anticoagulation, or eculizumab as appropriate.

Patients with active lupus nephritis should be counseled to avoid pregnancy while disease is active or potentially teratogenic treatment is ongoing, and for at least 6 months after lupus nephritis becomes inactive.
Hydroxychloroquine should be continued during pregnancy, and low-dose aspirin should be started before 16 weeks of gestation to reduce pregnancy complications.
Glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine, tacrolimus, and cyclosporine are considered safe immunosuppressive treatments during pregnancy.
Pediatric lupus nephritis should generally use immunosuppressive regimens similar to adult regimens, with attention to dose adjustment, growth, fertility, and psychosocial factors.
Patients with lupus nephritis who develop kidney failure may receive hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplantation, and kidney transplantation is preferred to long-term dialysis.
